c.tagline: Bolivia's booming tropical lowland hub, ringed by plazas and the gateway to the Jesuit Missions.

taxi.fareNote: Street taxis are unmetered - agree the fare before getting in, and use registered radio taxis or apps (Uber is limited here, Yango is common) for safety, especially after dark. Micros (city buses) and trufis (shared taxis on fixed routes) are the cheap local option.

emergency.note: 110 police, 118 ambulance/emergency medical, 119 fire. English-speaking operators are rare, so having Spanish help is useful.

hood_desc: The historic core around the leafy Plaza 24 de Septiembre and its cathedral, ringed by arcaded colonial streets, museums, markets, and the first of the city's concentric ring roads; the walkable base for first-timers.

Santa Cruz's most modern and upscale district just north of the center, packed with restaurants and cafes along pedestrian Avenida Monsenor Rivero, malls, and the city's liveliest nightlife on Avenida San Martin.
A quiet, leafy upscale residential enclave just beyond Equipetrol, with gated homes, boutique hotels, and easy access to the dining strip; calm but close to the action.
An affluent gated hillside suburb across the Pirai River, with country clubs, eco-resorts, and river views; a tranquil green retreat a short drive from downtown.
The sprawling northern commercial belt along Avenida Banzer and the outer ring roads, home to big shopping malls, chain hotels, and the airport road; convenient for shoppers and business travelers.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; avoid ice from unknown sources.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver - a micro or trufi ride is about Bs 2-2.50 (~$0.35); there is no smartcard system. Micros run fixed numbered routes across the ring roads, while trufis are shared taxis and minivans on set routes.
transit.hours: Micros and trufis run roughly 6am to 10-11pm; after that, radio taxis and ride apps fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Santa Cruz has no metro or tram. Public transport is entirely road-based: numbered micros (city buses) and trufis (shared taxis on fixed routes), supplemented by taxis and ride-hailing.

landmarks: Plaza 24 de Septiembre
Sloths once lounged in the trees of this leafy main square, still the tropical city's social hub ringed by cafes and colonial arcades.
Catedral Basílica de San Lorenzo
Climb the bell tower of this brick 19th-century cathedral for the best rooftop view over the plaza and sprawling lowland city.
Biocentro Güembé
A lush resort-style reserve of butterfly domes, orchid gardens, free-flying macaws and swimming lagoons on the city's edge.
Parque Regional Lomas de Arena
Improbable white sand dunes rise from lagoons and forest just south of the city, perfect for sandboarding and birdwatching.
Jardín Botánico de Santa Cruz
Trails through 186 hectares of preserved Chiquitano forest reveal sloths, turtles and towering cacti minutes from downtown.
El Fuerte de Samaipata
A UNESCO-listed pre-Inca ceremonial rock, the largest carved stone in the Americas, etched with jaguars and serpents in misty foothills.
Parque Nacional Amboró
One of Earth's most biodiverse parks, where Andes meets Amazon in waterfalls, giant ferns and 900 bird species, day-trippable from the city.
Manzana Uno Espacio de Arte
A free contemporary-art space in a restored colonial block beside the cathedral, showcasing Bolivia's liveliest rotating exhibitions.
Zoológico Municipal Noel Kempff Mercado
A conservation-minded zoo devoted to Bolivian species, from jaguars and tapirs to the endemic Bolivian river dolphin exhibits.
Santuario de la Virgen de Cotoca
Bolivia's eastern pilgrimage church shelters the miraculous Virgin of Cotoca, drawing thousands of walkers each December from Santa Cruz.

train.note: Ferroviaria Oriental runs the eastern-lowland railway from the Terminal Bimodal: east to Puerto Quijarro on the Brazilian border (connecting to Corumba) - the so-called 'Death Train' - and south toward Yacuiba on the Argentine border. Services reach the frontier towns rather than crossing directly.

intl.to: Yacuiba & Bermejo for Argentina, Puerto Suárez / Corumbá for Brazil, and Paraguay
intl.op: Terminal Bimodal coach operators — tickets at the terminal

bus.note: Long-distance and international coaches leave from the Terminal Bimodal, reaching Argentina (via Yacuiba/Bermejo), Brazil (via Puerto Suarez/Corumba), Paraguay, and other Bolivian cities such as Cochabamba, Sucre, and La Paz.

ferry.note: Santa Cruz lies deep inland on the Bolivian plain with no navigable waterway of its own, so there is no passenger ferry service. The nearest river ports are Puerto Quijarro and Puerto Suarez on the Paraguay River some 650 km east at the end of the Ferroviaria Oriental line, where cargo barges work down towards Paraguay but carry no scheduled passengers; travellers there cross to Corumba in Brazil by road instead.

full.name: Jesuit Missions of Chiquitos (San Javier)
full.blurb: The oldest of six UNESCO-listed Jesuit mission churches, with a wooden bell tower and baroque altar built by Chiquitano craftsmen.

full.name: Refugio Los Volcanes
full.blurb: A private nature reserve of red sandstone cliffs and cloud forest near Samaipata, with trails and swimming holes along a mountain stream.

full.name: Buena Vista
full.blurb: A small town at the edge of Amboró National Park with a colonial plaza, serving as a base for birdwatching and river trips.
